Hayao Miyazaki (born January 5, 1941) is a Japanese animator, filmmaker and manga artist who co-founded Studio Ghibli and serves as its honorary chairman, and is widely regarded as one of the greatest filmmakers in animation history.

His career began at Toei Animation in 1963 — where he formed a lifelong collaboration with Isao Takahata — before his feature debut The Castle of Cagliostro (1979), and after founding Studio Ghibli in 1985 he directed beloved films including My Neighbor Totoro (1988), Princess Mononoke (1997, the first animated film to win the Japan Academy Prize for Picture of the Year), and Spirited Away (2001, which won the Academy Award for Best Animated Feature).

He briefly retired in 2013 but returned with The Boy and the Heron (2023), another Oscar winner, and his films — known for themes of nature, pacifism, craftsmanship and strong young heroines — continue to influence animators and filmmakers worldwide.
